proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(d\geq1\), \(E\geq d+2\), and \(R_{\max}\geq d+2\).  The already established environment-sharpness theorem shows that \(E\geq d+2\) is exactly the environmental regime in which a finite breakout can occur.  We now construct, with one collection of bounds for all admissible \(r\), unequal-effect pairs that cannot be distinguished by lower-order mixed moments.

For \(r\in\{d+2,\ldots,R_{\max}\}\), define
\[
 \nu_{rj}=(-1)^{r-j}{r\choose j},\qquad 1\leq j\leq r.
\]
The identity
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{r}(-1)^{r-j}{r\choose j}e^{jx}=(e^x-1)^r
 \tag{1}
\]
is the binomial theorem applied to \(e^x-1\).  Differentiating (1) \(k\) times at zero gives
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{r}\nu_{rj}j^k=0\quad(1\leq k<r),
 \qquad
 \sum_{j=1}^{r}\nu_{rj}j^r=r!.
 \tag{2}
\]
Thus the signed measure with masses \(\nu_{rj}\) at \(j\) annihilates every positive-order monomial below degree \(r\), but not the degree-\(r\) monomial.

Put
\[
 K=\max_{d+2\leq s\leq R_{\max}}\max_{1\leq j\leq s}|\nu_{sj}|<\infty
\]
and fix \(\eta>0\) and \(0<\varepsilon<(2K)^{-1}\).  Let \(L\) vary in \([1,2]\).  For \(1\leq j\leq R_{\max}\) and \(e\in\mathcal E\), define baseline intensities
\[
 \Lambda^{V}_{e,j}=L+\eta\mathbf 1\{1\leq e=j\leq d\},
 \qquad
 \Lambda^{W}_{e,j}=L+2\eta\mathbf 1\{1\leq e=j\leq d\}.
 \tag{3}
\]
For an intensity vector \(\Lambda=(\Lambda_1,\ldots,\Lambda_{R_{\max}})\) and \(\sigma^2>0\), let
\[
 X(\Lambda,\sigma^2)
 =G_{\sigma}+
   \sum_{j=1}^{R_{\max}}j\{N_j-\Lambda_j\},
 \tag{4}
\]
where \(G_{\sigma}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\), the variables \(N_j\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\Lambda_j)\) are independent, and the Gaussian variable is independent of all the counts.  Its log moment generating function is
\[
 \log\mathbb E e^{xX(\Lambda,\sigma^2)}
 =\frac{\sigma^2x^2}{2}
  +\sum_{j=1}^{R_{\max}}\Lambda_j(e^{jx}-1-jx),
 \tag{5}
\]
which is finite for every real \(x\).  Formula (4) is centered, and differentiating (5) shows that for every \(k\geq2\),
\[
 \kappa_k\{X(\Lambda,\sigma^2)\}
 =\sigma^2\mathbf 1\{k=2\}+
   \sum_{j=1}^{R_{\max}}\Lambda_jj^k.
 \tag{6}
\]

Choose \((\sigma_V^2,\sigma_W^2,\sigma_y^2)\in[1,2]^3\).  Let \(V_e^\circ\) and \(W_e^\circ\) have the laws in (4) with intensities \(\Lambda^V_e\) and \(\Lambda^W_e\), and variances \(\sigma_V^2\) and \(\sigma_W^2\), respectively.  Let \(Z\sim N(0,\sigma_y^2)\).  All sources are chosen mutually independent within each environment.  Consider first the two unperturbed structural representations
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccc|ccc}
 &\alpha&\beta&\gamma&\epsilon_{u,e}&\epsilon_{t,e}&\epsilon_y\\ \hline
 \theta_0^\circ&1&2&1&V_e^\circ&W_e^\circ&Z\\
 \theta_1^\circ&1&3&-1&W_e^\circ&V_e^\circ&Z.
 \end{array}
 \tag{7}
\]
The second row is the exact source swap \(S\theta_0^\circ\).  More directly, the structural equations give in both rows
\[
 T_e=V_e^\circ+W_e^\circ,
 \qquad
 Y_e=3V_e^\circ+2W_e^\circ+Z.
 \tag{8}
\]
Hence the complete baseline observed laws, not merely selected moments, coincide.

Fix an admissible \(r\).  Because \(E\geq d+2\), the environment \(e=d+1\) exists.  Form \(W_e^{(r)}\) from \(W_e^\circ\) by replacing, only when \(e=d+1\), its jump-\(j\) intensity by
\[
 \Lambda^W_{d+1,j}+\varepsilon\nu_{rj}\mathbf 1\{j\leq r\}.
 \tag{9}
\]
Define \(V_e^{(r)}\) analogously from \(V_e^\circ\).  Every intensity in (9) is at least
\[
 1-\varepsilon K>\frac12,
 \tag{10}
\]
so both perturbations are probability laws of the form (4), rather than signed laws.  Define
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccc|ccc}
 &\alpha&\beta&\gamma&\epsilon_{u,e}&\epsilon_{t,e}&\epsilon_y\\ \hline
 \theta_{0,r}&1&2&1&V_e^\circ&W_e^{(r)}&Z\\
 \theta_{1,r}&1&3&-1&W_e^\circ&V_e^{(r)}&Z.
 \end{array}
 \tag{11}
\]
Thus the order-specific perturbation is always placed in the treatment noise.  In particular, it does not alter either latent cumulant profile.

We next prove lower-order observational equality.  Define the entire function
\[
 H_r(x)=\varepsilon\sum_{j=1}^{r}\nu_{rj}(e^{jx}-1-jx).
 \tag{12}
\]
By (2), every derivative of \(H_r\) at zero of order smaller than \(r\) vanishes, whereas
\[
 H_r^{(r)}(0)=\varepsilon r!.
 \tag{13}
\]
Let \(M_e^\circ(s,t)\) denote the common joint moment generating function of the baseline pair in (8).  Outside the spare environment, the observed laws in (11) equal their respective baseline laws and hence agree.  In the spare environment, independence, (5), and the coefficients with which the perturbed treatment source enters \((T,Y)\) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 M_{0,d+1}(s,t)&=M_{d+1}^\circ(s,t)\exp\{H_r(s+2t)\},\\
 M_{1,d+1}(s,t)&=M_{d+1}^\circ(s,t)\exp\{H_r(s+3t)\}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{14}
\]
Equations (12)--(13) imply that \(H_r(x)=x^rg_r(x)\) for an entire \(g_r\).  Consequently, each exponential factor in (14) equals one plus an analytic function all of whose monomials have total degree at least \(r\).  Taking \(p\) derivatives in \(s\) and \(\ell\) derivatives in \(t\) at \((0,0)\), and using that derivatives of a joint moment generating function are mixed moments, yields
\[
 \mathbb E_{\theta_{0,r}}[T_e^pY_e^\ell]
 =\mathbb E_{\theta_{1,r}}[T_e^pY_e^\ell]
 \quad
 \text{for every }e\in\mathcal E\text{ and }p+\ell<r.
 \tag{15}
\]
This also covers total degrees zero and one because the laws are normalized and the sources are centered.

It remains to verify the calibration plane, the first breakout, and uniform membership in one bounded model.  By (3), (6), and (2), the treatment cumulant contrasts of either member of (11) are, for every \(k\geq2\),
\[
 c_k
 =3\eta\sum_{j=1}^{d}j^k\mathbf e_j
  +h_{r,k}\mathbf e_{d+1},
 \qquad
 h_{r,k}=\varepsilon\sum_{j=1}^{r}\nu_{rj}j^k.
 \tag{16}
\]
In particular, \(h_{r,k}=0\) for \(2\leq k<r\), and \(h_{r,r}=\varepsilon r!\).  Since \(r\geq d+2\), the calibration matrix is
\[
 C=3\eta
 \begin{bmatrix}
 V_d\\
 0_{(E-1-d)\times d}
 \end{bmatrix},
 \qquad
 V_d=[j^k]_{j=1,\ldots,d;\ k=2,\ldots,d+1}.
 \tag{17}
\]
Factoring \(j^2\) from row \(j\) reduces \(V_d\) to the ordinary Vandermonde matrix, so
\[
 \det(V_d)=
 \left(\prod_{j=1}^{d}j^2\right)
 \left(\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq d}(j-i)\right)\neq0.
 \tag{18}
\]
Therefore \(C\) has rank \(d\),
\[
 A=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf e_1,\ldots,\mathbf e_d\},
 \qquad
 \sigma_d(C)=3\eta\sigma_d(V_d)>0,
 \tag{19}
\]
and \(Q_A\) deletes precisely the first \(d\) coordinates.  Moreover, the latent profiles in (11) are
\[
 u_k(\theta_{0,r})=\eta\sum_{j=1}^{d}j^k\mathbf e_j,
 \qquad
 u_k(\theta_{1,r})=2\eta\sum_{j=1}^{d}j^k\mathbf e_j,
 \tag{20}
\]
for every \(k\geq2\).  Thus both profiles belong to \(A\) at every order.  Finally, (2) and (16) give
\[
 Q_Ac_k=0\quad(d+2\leq k<r),
 \qquad
 Q_Ac_r=\varepsilon r!\mathbf e_{d+1}\neq0.
 \tag{21}
\]
By the definition of the first breakout, (21) proves
\[
 r^\star(\theta_{0,r})=r^\star(\theta_{1,r})=r.
 \tag{22}
\]

Choose the fixed coefficient bounds
\[
 B=4,qquad a_0=\frac12,qquad a_1=\frac32,qquad
 q_0=\frac12,qquad q_1=\frac32,
 \tag{23}
\]
and choose
\[
 \kappa_0=\frac32\eta\sigma_d(V_d)>0.
 \tag{24}
\]
Both rows of (11) satisfy the effect, treatment-loading, and two-sided confounding bounds because their coefficient triples are \((1,2,1)\) and \((1,3,-1)\).  Equations (18)--(20) verify the calibration-rank, calibration-gap, and latent-profile-plane conditions.  Centering and within-environment source independence hold by construction, and (5) verifies the entire-moment-generating-function condition.

For completeness, one moment envelope works for every \(r\) and every parameter value just used.  Across the finite collection of orders, all intensities are bounded above by \(2+2\eta+\varepsilon K\), all jumps are bounded by \(R_{\max}\), and all Gaussian variances are at most two.  Hence (5) is bounded uniformly over this collection at \(x=1\) and \(x=-1\).  For \(s=2R_{\max}+\delta\), the elementary bound
\[
 |x|^s\leq C_s(e^x+e^{-x}),
 \qquad
 C_s=\sup_{z\geq0}z^se^{-z}<\infty,
 \tag{25}
\]
therefore gives a finite uniform upper bound on the required absolute source moments.  Choose \(M\) strictly larger than this bound.  The same \(M\), the same \(\kappa_0\), and the coefficient bounds in (23) apply to every \(r\).  Thus each parameter in (11) belongs to this single \(\Theta\), and (22), together with \(d+2\leq r\leq R_{\max}\), puts it in \(\mathcal B\).

For each \(r\), let \(L\) and the three Gaussian variances range over \([1,2]^4\), and include both rows of (11).  This is a finite-dimensional subclass with nonempty continuous parameter rectangles; its compound-Poisson intensities are strictly positive by (10), and its Gaussian components have strictly positive variances.  It is therefore a nondegenerate Poisson--Gaussian subclass of \(\mathcal B\).  Choosing the same interior rectangle point in its two rows gives members \(\theta_0=\theta_{0,r}\) and \(\theta_1=\theta_{1,r}\) for which (15) and (22) hold, while
\[
 \beta(\theta_0)=2\neq3=\beta(\theta_1).
\]
Because all bounds and the subclass parameter rectangle were chosen independently of \(r\), this proves the claim with one fixed compatible bounded model.

proposed.statement: For every \(d\geq1\), \(E\geq d+2\), and \(R_{\max}\geq d+2\), there is one fixed compatible choice of the bounded model \(\Theta\), common to all \(r\in\{d+2,\ldots,R_{\max}\}\), such that for every such \(r\) the resulting \(\mathcal B\) contains a nondegenerate finite-dimensional Poisson--Gaussian subclass and two members \(\theta_0,\theta_1\) satisfying \(\beta(\theta_0)\neq\beta(\theta_1)\), \(r^\star(\theta_0)=r^\star(\theta_1)=r\), and \(\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[T_e^pY_e^{\ell}]=\mathbb E_{\theta_1}[T_e^pY_e^{\ell}]\) for every \(e\in\mathcal E\) and every \(p,\ell\geq0\) with \(p+\ell<r\).
proposed.justification: The first breakout order is information-theoretically meaningful, not an artifact of one estimator's search loop.
proposed.gap: Existing cumulant methods assume a useful nonzero order; they do not construct legal unequal-effect SEMs that match every lower observed mixed moment and become identified exactly at the prescribed order.
proposed.consumer: The theorem prevents analysts from truncating the moment search below \(r\) while claiming uniform identification over delayed-breakout environments.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The completed proof explicitly verifies ambient-class membership and the breakout-branch conditions, so the target's dependency metadata must expose the corresponding frozen assumptions and definitions.

proofs.proof_tex:
Assume \(d=1\) and \(E=2\).  Then \(E=d+1\).  By the rank assumption \(\operatorname{rank}(C)=d=1\), the hypotheses of \(\text{thm:environment-sharpness}\) apply.  Its boundary conclusion gives
\[
A=\mathbb R^d=\mathbb R
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
Q_A=0.
\]
Equivalently, writing the one-by-one calibration matrix as \(C=[c_2]\), rank one implies \(c_2\ne0\), so \(C^\top C=c_2^2>0\) and
\[
Q_A
=I_1-C(C^\top C)^{-1}C^\top
=1-c_2(c_2^2)^{-1}c_2
=0.
\]
Thus \(Q_Ac_k=0\) for every integer \(k\ge3=d+2\).  Hence the set \(\{k\ge d+2:Q_Ac_k\ne0\}\) is empty and the first-breakout convention yields \(r^\star=\infty\).  In particular no parameter satisfying the calibration condition can have a finite breakout, and therefore the finite-breakout branch obeys
\[
\mathcal B=\varnothing.
\]

Now let \(\theta\in\mathcal N_\rho\).  The already established \(\text{thm:identification-frontier}\), applied to this no-breakout parameter, states that \(\theta\) and \(S\theta\) induce the same observed law in every environment:
\[
P_e^{\theta}=P_e^{S\theta}
\qquad(e\in\mathcal E).
\]
By the source-swap definition, their direct treatment effects are respectively
\[
\beta(\theta)=\beta,
\qquad
\beta(S\theta)=\beta+\frac{\gamma}{\alpha}.
\]
The same frontier theorem states that these two effects are distinct; its conclusion uses the maintained nonzero-confounding bound in the ambient model.  Moreover, membership in \(\mathcal N_\rho\) makes this a legal swap pair, and the theorem places both representations in \(\mathcal D_\rho\).  Consequently every nonempty surviving no-breakout branch exhibits observational equivalence with unequal causal effects.  This is exactly the simultaneous-source ambiguity asserted by the proposition at the two-environment boundary; the reference to Kivva et al., Theorem 3.6, is a comparison of scope and is not used as a proof premise.

The structural causal target is the coefficient \(\beta\): under the intervention that sets treatment to \(t\), the structural equation gives
\[
Y_e(t)=\beta t+\gamma U_e+\epsilon_y,
\]
so the unit change in the interventional outcome holding the exogenous variables fixed is \(\beta\).  This is distinct from the observable cumulant quotient.  The already established cumulant-cancellation lemma and identification-frontier theorem prove that, on a finite-breakout law, the quotient equals this structural target.  We now establish the statistical assertions.

Put \(s_0=2R_{\max}+\delta\).  From the treatment-loading, confounding, effect, and source-moment bounds,
\[
 |\gamma|=|\alpha|\,|\gamma/\alpha|\leq a_1q_1,
\]
and Minkowski's inequality in \(L^{s_0}\), applied to the two structural equations, gives a finite constant \(K_0\), depending only on the fixed model bounds, such that
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{e\in\mathcal E}
 \mathbb E_\theta\!left[|T_e|^{s_0}+|Y_e|^{s_0}\right]\leq K_0. \tag{1}
\]
Here the division in \(\gamma/\alpha\) is licensed by \(|\alpha|\geq a_0>0\).  In particular, all moments used below exist uniformly.

We first verify the stochastic accuracy of the stipulated cumulant statistics.  If \(X_1,\ldots,X_k\) are coordinates, each equal to \(T_e\) or \(Y_e\), coefficient comparison in the finite-degree part of the formal identity \(\log(1+x)=\sum_{j\geq1}(-1)^{j-1}x^j/j\), applied to the joint moment generating function, yields
\[
 \operatorname{cum}(X_1,\ldots,X_k)
 =\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak P_k}(|\pi|-1)!(-1)^{|\pi|-1}
   \prod_{D\in\pi}\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j\in D}X_j\right], \tag{2}
\]
where \(\mathfrak P_k\) is the finite set of partitions of \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\).  For \(\pi=\{D_1,\ldots,D_s\}\), an unbiased estimator of the product in (2) is
\[
 \frac{1}{(n_e)_s}
 \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_s\ {
m distinct}}
 \prod_{a=1}^s\prod_{j\in D_a}X_{j,e,i_a}. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, independence of distinct observations makes the expectation of every summand in (3) equal to the corresponding product of moments.  Symmetrizing the finite sum of (3) over the partitions in (2) gives exactly an admissible symmetrized unbiased cumulant U-statistic from the estimator definition.

The square of a summand in (3) has total degree at most \(2k\leq2R_{\max}<s_0\).  Thus (1), Lyapunov's inequality, and H\"older's inequality bound its second moment uniformly.  In the variance double sum, two summands based on disjoint observation-index sets are independent and have zero covariance.  For a fixed \(s\), only \(O(n_e^{2s-1})\) of the \(O(n_e^{2s})\) ordered pairs overlap.  Since the number of partitions, environments, and admitted orders is fixed, the balanced-share condition \(n_e\geq\underline\pi n\) gives a constant \(K_1<\infty\) for which, whenever all \(n_e\geq R_{\max}\),
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \mathbb E_\theta\!\left[
 \|\widehat c_k-c_k\|_2^2+\|\widehat m_k-m_k\|_2^2
 \right]\leq \frac{K_1}{n},
 \qquad 2\leq k\leq R_{\max}. \tag{4}
\]
The same finite polynomial formula (2), together with (1), also supplies uniform deterministic bounds on \(\|c_k\|_2\) and \(\|m_k\|_2\).

Let \(H=\widehat C-C\), and let \(\widehat A\) be the rank-\(d\) left singular subspace used to define \(\widehat Q\).  On the event \(\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\kappa_0/2\), if \(x=Cy\) is a unit vector in \(A\), then \(\|y\|_2\leq\kappa_0^{-1}\) and
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(x,\widehat A)
 \leq\|Hy\|_2\leq\kappa_0^{-1}\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}. \tag{5}
\]
Moreover, directly from the variational definition of a singular value,
\[
 \sigma_d(\widehat C)
 \geq\sigma_d(C)-\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \geq\kappa_0/2. \tag{6}
\]
Consequently, if \(z=\widehat Cy\) is a unit vector in \(\widehat A\), then \(\|y\|_2\leq2/\kappa_0\) and
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(z,A)\leq2\kappa_0^{-1}\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}. \tag{7}
\]
For completeness, decomposing a vector into its projections on two equal-dimensional subspaces bounds the operator norm of the difference of their orthogonal projectors by the sum of the two directed distances in (5) and (7).  Since \(Q_A\) and \(\widehat Q\) are the complementary projectors, (5)--(7) imply the convenient bound
\[
 \|\widehat Q-Q_A\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq\frac{4}{\kappa_0}\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}. \tag{8}
\]
On the complementary event, the left side is at most two.  Equation (4), applied to the fixed \(d\) columns of \(H\), and Markov's inequality therefore give
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \mathbb E_\theta\|\widehat Q-Q_A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
 \leq\frac{K_2}{n} \tag{9}
\]
for another uniform constant \(K_2\).  This argument does not invert an influence covariance and remains valid when that covariance is singular.

For \(|b|\leq B\), define the proof intermediates
\[
 g_k(b)=Q_A(m_k-bc_k),\qquad
 \widehat g_k(b)=\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-b\widehat c_k),
\]
and
\[
 \Delta_n=\max_{d+2\leq k\leq R_{\max}}
 \sup_{|b|\leq B}\|\widehat g_k(b)-g_k(b)\|_2.
\]
The exact decomposition
\[
 \widehat g_k(b)-g_k(b)
 =\widehat Q\{(\widehat m_k-m_k)-b(\widehat c_k-c_k)\}
  +(\widehat Q-Q_A)(m_k-bc_k) \tag{10}
\]
combined with (4), (9), the population bounds following (4), and the finiteness of the admitted order set yields
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\Delta_n^2\leq\frac{K_3}{n}. \tag{11}
\]
Thus (11) includes the generated-projector error rather than treating the plane as known.

By the cumulant-cancellation lemma, for every \(\theta\in\mathcal D_\rho\),
\[
 g_k(b)=(\beta-b)Q_Ac_k,
 \qquad g_k(\beta)=0. \tag{12}
\]
This is the step relating the observable moments to the causal target.  If \(\theta\in\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)\), the defining optimization and (10)--(12) imply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\widehat\beta-\beta|\,\|Q_Ac_r\|_2
 &=\|g_r(\widehat\beta)\|_2\\
 &\leq \|\widehat g_r(\widehat\beta)\|_2+\Delta_n\\
 &\leq \max_k\|\widehat g_k(\widehat\beta)\|_2+\Delta_n\\
 &\leq \max_k\|\widehat g_k(\beta)\|_2+\Delta_n
 \leq2\Delta_n.
 \end{aligned} \tag{13}
\]
The minimizer exists because the objective is continuous on the compact interval \([-B,B]\).  Since the shell has \(\|Q_Ac_r\|_2\geq\lambda_n\), while both \(\widehat\beta\) and \(\beta\) lie in \([-B,B]\), (11)--(13) give
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)}
 \mathbb E_\theta(\widehat\beta-\beta)^2
 \leq K_4\min\!\left\{B^2,\frac{1}{n\lambda_n^2}\right\}. \tag{14}
\]

Choose the deterministic radius in the Anderson--Rubin definition so that
\[
 t_{\alpha_0}^2\geq K_3/\alpha_0. \tag{15}
\]
Let \(\mathcal R_n\) denote the raw norm-sublevel set appearing in that definition.  On \(\{\Delta_n\leq t_{\alpha_0}/\sqrt n\}\), (12) puts \(\beta\) in \(\mathcal R_n\).  Equations (11), (15), and Markov's inequality therefore imply
\[
 \inf_{\theta\in\mathcal D_\rho}
 \Pr_\theta\{\beta\in\mathcal C_n\}\geq1-\alpha_0. \tag{16}
\]
Indeed, on this event the raw set cannot be empty, so the singleton fallback does not affect coverage.  The small-sample fallback \([-B,B]\) covers identically.

Every constraint defining \(\mathcal R_n\) is a convex sublevel set of the norm of an affine function of the scalar \(b\); hence their intersection with \([-B,B]\) is an interval.  If \(b,b'\in\mathcal R_n\), then (10)--(12) and the shell lower bound give
\[
 |b-b'|\lambda_n
 \leq\|g_r(b)-g_r(b')\|_2
 \leq2\left(\frac{t_{\alpha_0}}{\sqrt n}+\Delta_n\right). \tag{17}
\]
If \(\mathcal R_n\) is empty, the prescribed fallback is a singleton and has length zero.  Thus the box bound, (11), (17), and Cauchy--Schwarz yield
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)}
 \mathbb E_\theta\operatorname{length}(\mathcal C_n)
 \leq K_5\min\!\left\{B,\frac{1}{\sqrt n\lambda_n}\right\}. \tag{18}
\]
Both (13) and (17) use the true \(r\) only in the analysis; the estimator and interval maximize over all admitted orders and therefore do not require knowledge of \(r\).

It remains only to cover the finitely many sample sizes at which some \(n_e<R_{\max}\).  Balanced shares imply that this can occur only when \(n<R_{\max}/\underline\pi\).  Formula (2) and (1) give a uniform constant \(\Lambda<\infty\) with \(\|Q_Ac_k\|_2\leq\Lambda\).  The deterministic error and length bounds \(B^2\) and \(2B\), together with \(\lambda_n\leq\Lambda\) for a nonempty shell, show that increasing \(K_4,K_5\) makes (14) and (18) valid also for these finitely many \(n\).

We next construct one fixed compatible experiment giving both lower bounds, uniformly over the finite set of possible \(r\).  Fix arbitrary \(d\geq1\), \(E\geq d+2\), and \(R_{\max}\geq d+2\).  Set
\[
 J=[19/10,23/10],\qquad
 \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&5\\5&14\end{pmatrix},
\]
and, for \(b\in J\), define
\[
 f_b=\frac{5-2b}{3-b},\qquad
 g_b=\frac{1}{3-b},\qquad z_b=b-1. \tag{19}
\]
All denominators and all three quantities in (19) are bounded away from zero on \(J\).  Let \(V_b,W_b,Z_b\) be independent centered Gaussian variables with variances \(f_b,g_b,z_b\), respectively.  Direct algebra gives
\[
 f_b+g_b=2,\qquad 3f_b+bg_b=5,\qquad
 9f_b+b^2g_b+z_b=14, \tag{20}
\]
and hence
\[
 G_b=(V_b+W_b,\,3V_b+bW_b+Z_b)\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma) \tag{21}
\]
for every \(b\in J\).

Independently, construct
\[
 L_e=\sum_{j=1}^d j(N_{e,j}-\lambda_{e,j}),
\]
where the independent Poisson rates have a common positive baseline and the jump-\(j\) rate is increased by a fixed \(\eta>0\) only in environment \(e=j\); environments \(e>d\) retain the baseline rates.  Define the structural sources and coefficients by
\[
 \epsilon_{u,e}=L_e+V_b,\qquad
 \epsilon_{t,e}=W_b,\qquad
 \epsilon_y=Z_b,qquad
 \alpha=1,\qquad \beta=b,\qquad \gamma=3-b. \tag{22}
\]
Before the perturbation introduced below, the observed variables satisfy
\[
 (T_e,Y_e)=(L_e,3L_e)+G_b, \tag{23}
\]
so their entire joint law is independent of \(b\), not merely their covariance.  The latent cumulant-shift vector at order \(k\) is
\[
 u_k=\eta(1^k,\ldots,d^k,0,\ldots,0)^\top,
\]
because the added Gaussian component is invariant across environments.  Consequently the calibration matrix has leading block \(\eta V_d\), its column space is
\(A=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf e_1,\ldots,\mathbf e_d\}\), and \(u_k\in A\) at every order.

For an admitted \(r\), let \(\operatorname{He}_r\) be the probabilists' Hermite polynomial and set
\[
 h_r(x)=e^{-x^2}\operatorname{He}_r(\sqrt3x),
 \qquad \mu_r=\frac{r!}{3^{(r+1)/2}}. \tag{24}
\]
Both \(h_r\) and its derivative are bounded.  If \(N\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), the substitution \(u=\sqrt3x\) and the Rodrigues identity, followed by \(r\) integrations by parts, give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E[N^kh_r(N)]
 &=3^{-(k+1)/2}\mathbb E[N^k\operatorname{He}_r(N)]\\
 &=\begin{cases}
 0,&0\leq k<r,\\
 \mu_r,&k=r.
 \end{cases}
 \end{aligned} \tag{25}
\]
Every boundary term is zero because a polynomial times a Gaussian density tends to zero at both endpoints.

Only in the spare environment \(e=d+1\), replace the density of \(W_b\) by
\[
 p_{b,\lambda}(w)=\phi_{g_b}(w)
 \left\{1+\frac{\lambda}{\mu_rg_b^{r/2}}
 h_r\!\left(\frac{w}{\sqrt{g_b}}\right)\right\}. \tag{26}
\]
Because \(J\) is compact and the admitted set of \(r\)'s is finite, there is one \(\lambda_0>0\), common to all \(r\), such that the bracket in (26) lies in \([1/2,3/2]\) whenever \(0<\lambda\leq\lambda_0\).  Equation (25), first with \(k=0\) and then with \(k=1\), proves respectively that (26) integrates to one and remains centered.  More generally, (25) shows that all raw moments below order \(r\) are unchanged and that the order-\(r\) raw moment increases by exactly \(\lambda\).  Since the order-\(r\) cumulant is the order-\(r\) moment plus a polynomial in lower moments, (2) proves that the order-\(r\) cumulant also increases by exactly \(\lambda\).  Gaussian domination of (26) gives an entire moment generating function and uniform moments of every fixed order.

Because \(r\geq d+2\), this perturbation leaves every column of \(C\) unchanged.  The lower-order projected contrasts vanish, whereas at order \(r\),
\[
 Q_Ac_r=\lambda\mathbf e_{d+1},\qquad
 Q_Am_r=b\lambda\mathbf e_{d+1}. \tag{27}
\]
The second equality follows either directly from multilinearity and independence of the structural sources, or from cumulant cancellation.  Choose once and for all \(B>23/10\), coefficient bounds containing \(\alpha=1\) and \(\gamma=3-b\) for \(b\in J\), a gap \(\kappa_0<\eta\sigma_d(V_d)\), and a moment envelope larger than the compact supremum over \(b\in J\), \(0\leq\lambda\leq\lambda_0\), and the finite set of admitted \(r\)'s.  The Poisson and Gaussian sources are centered, mutually independent, and have entire moment generating functions.  Thus all ambient-class assumptions, including the latent-plane and calibration conditions, hold with fixed constants, and (27) places every resulting law in \(\mathcal M_r(\lambda)\).  This constructs one fixed compatible \(\Theta\), common to all \(r\).

We bound the divergence of the full observed-data laws, so the lower bound is not an artifact of moment compression.  Under the unperturbed Gaussian law (21), Gaussian completion of squares gives
\[
 \mathbb E_b[W_b\mid G_b=x]=\ell_b^\top x,
 \qquad \ell_b^\top=g_b(1,b)\Sigma^{-1}, \tag{28}
\]
and
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \tau_b^2
 &=\operatorname{Var}_b(W_b\mid G_b)\\
 &=g_b-g_b^2(1,b)\Sigma^{-1}(1,b)^\top
 =-\frac{(b-1)(2b-5)}{3(b-3)^2}>0.
 \end{aligned} \tag{29}
\]
The strict positivity in (29) is uniform on \(J\).  Conditioning the likelihood ratio in (26) on \(G_b=x\) shows that the perturbed density of \(G_b\) is
\[
 \phi_\Sigma(x)\{1+\lambda R_b(x)\},
\]
where
\[
 R_b(x)=\frac{1}{\mu_rg_b^{r/2}}
 \mathbb E\!\left[
 h_r\!\left(\frac{\ell_b^\top x+\tau_bN}{\sqrt{g_b}}\right)
 \right]. \tag{30}
\]
The coefficient functions in (28)--(30) are continuously differentiable on \(J\), and \(g_b,\tau_b\) are bounded away from zero.  Boundedness of \(h_r,h_r'\) permits differentiation under the standard-normal expectation, with dominating variable \(K(1+\|x\|_2+|N|)\).  Uniformly over the finite set of \(r\)'s,
\[
 |R_b(x)|\leq K_6,
 \qquad |\partial_bR_b(x)|\leq K_7(1+\|x\|_2). \tag{31}
\]
The mean-value theorem and the finite second moment of \(\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)\) now imply
\[
 \int\{R_b(x)-R_{b'}(x)\}^2\phi_\Sigma(x)\,dx
 \leq K_8|b-b'|^2. \tag{32}
\]
After decreasing \(\lambda_0\) so that \(\lambda_0K_6\leq1/2\), direct substitution of the two densities into the chi-square divergence gives
\[
 \chi^2(P^G_{b,\lambda},P^G_{b',\lambda})
 \leq2K_8\lambda^2|b-b'|^2. \tag{33}
\]
Adding the independent \(L_e\) and applying the common measurable map in (23) cannot increase chi-square divergence: the image likelihood ratio is the conditional expectation of the original likelihood ratio, so conditional Jensen's inequality applies to its squared centered value.  All environments other than \(d+1\) have a law independent of \(b\).  Independence across observations and \(1+x\leq e^x\) therefore yield
\[
 1+\chi^2(P_{b,\lambda}^{,n},P_{b',\lambda}^{,n})
 \leq\exp\{K_9n\lambda^2|b-b'|^2\}. \tag{34}
\]
For any two dominated laws, Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 =\frac12\int\left|\frac{dP}{dQ}-1\right|dQ
 \leq\frac12\sqrt{\chi^2(P,Q)}. \tag{35}
\]

Fix \(b_0=2\), and put
\[
 h_n=c\min\!\left\{B,\frac{1}{\sqrt n\lambda}\right\},
 \qquad b_1=b_0+h_n. \tag{36}
\]
Choose the fixed \(c>0\) small enough that \(b_1\in J\) and that (34)--(35) imply
\[
 \|P_{b_0,\lambda}^{,n}-P_{b_1,\lambda}^{,n}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \leq v<\min\{1/2,1-2\alpha_0\} \tag{37}
\]
for all \(0<\lambda\leq\lambda_0\).  For an arbitrary estimator, let \(D\) be the event on which it is closer to \(b_0\) than to \(b_1\).  On \(D^c\) its squared error under the first law is at least \(h_n^2/4\), and on \(D\) its squared error under the second law is at least \(h_n^2/4\).  The definition of total variation then gives
\[
 \max_{j=0,1}\mathbb E_{b_j,\lambda}
 (\widetilde\beta-b_j)^2
 \geq\frac{h_n^2}{8}(1-v). \tag{38}
\]
If a random interval \(\mathcal I_n\) covers each parameter with probability at least \(1-\alpha_0\), then under the first law the events \(\{b_0\in\mathcal I_n\}\) and \(\{b_1\in\mathcal I_n\}\) have intersection probability at least \(1-2\alpha_0-v\).  On their intersection, interval connectedness forces length at least \(h_n\).  Hence
\[
 \mathbb E_{b_0,\lambda}\operatorname{length}(\mathcal I_n)
 \geq h_n(1-2\alpha_0-v). \tag{39}
\]
Both laws in (38)--(39) belong to the same shell, so these bounds apply even when honesty is required only on that shell.

For signals bounded away from zero, the same fixed \(\Theta\) contains a standard parametric path.  Indeed, (1)--(2) give the fixed upper bound \(\Lambda\) already used above, so a nonempty shell must have \(\lambda\leq\Lambda\).  If \(\lambda_0\leq\lambda\leq\Lambda\), take a member of the nonempty shell, retain its \(\alpha\), latent sources, and treatment sources, choose a fixed \(q\in(q_0,q_1)\), put \(\gamma=\alpha q\), take an independent centered Gaussian \(\epsilon_y\) with a fixed sufficiently small positive variance \(\sigma_y^2\), and vary \(\beta\) over a fixed interior subinterval of \([-B,B]\).  These changes leave \(C,A,r^\star\), and the shell strength unchanged and preserve every ambient-class assumption.  In the more informative experiment observing \((U,T,Y)\), two effects separated by \(h\) have
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(P_\beta^n,P_{\beta+h}^n)
 =\frac{h^2}{2\sigma_y^2}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}n_e\mathbb E[T_e^2]
 \leq K_{10}nh^2. \tag{40}
\]
Marginalizing \(U\) can only decrease relative entropy, again by conditional Jensen's inequality applied to the image likelihood ratio.  To relate (40) to total variation without an additional premise, apply data processing to the binary indicator of an event attaining total variation.  The resulting binary relative entropy, as a function of its first success probability, has second derivative at least four; Taylor's theorem gives
\(\operatorname{KL}(P,Q)\geq2\|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}^2\).  Taking \(h=c\min\{B,n^{-1/2}\}\) with \(c\) small and repeating (38)--(39) proves lower bounds of orders
\[
 \min\{B^2,n^{-1}\}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \min\{B,n^{-1/2}\}. \tag{41}
\]
Because \(\lambda\in[\lambda_0,\Lambda]\), the two expressions in (41) are, up to constants depending only on the fixed experiment, respectively equivalent to
\[
 \min\!\left\{B^2,\frac{1}{n\lambda^2}\right\}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \min\!\left\{B,\frac{1}{\sqrt n\lambda}\right\}. \tag{42}
\]

Taking the infimum in (38) over all estimators and the infimum in (39) over all intervals honest on the shell, and combining the resulting lower bounds with (14) and (18), proves the asserted two minimax orders on the single fixed compatible experiment.  Uniform coverage on \(\mathcal D_\rho\) is stronger than shell-only coverage, so the same interval lower bound applies to intervals honest on \(\mathcal D_\rho\).

Finally, if \(\sqrt n\lambda_n\to\infty\), (14) proves uniform mean-square, hence uniform probabilistic, consistency of \(\widehat\beta\) along every nonempty shell sequence.  Conversely, if this divergence fails, some subsequence has \(\sqrt n\lambda_n\) bounded.  Along that subsequence \(\lambda_n\to0\), so eventually \(\lambda_n\leq\lambda_0\), and (36)--(38) bound the minimax squared risk away from zero.  No uniformly consistent estimator exists on that subsequence.  This proves the stated if-and-only-if frontier.

Fix an arbitrary triangular array in \(\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)\), and suppress the array index \(n\) on population quantities when no confusion can result.  All bounds below are uniform over this array.  The frozen sampling design says that the observations are independent within and across environments and that, within environment \(e\), the variables \(W_{e,i}=(T_{e,i},Y_{e,i})\), \(1\leq i\leq n_e\), are identically distributed with law \(P_e\).  By balanced shares,
\[
 n_e=n\pi_e\geq n\underline\pi . \tag{1}
\]
Consequently, for all sufficiently large \(n\), every \(n_e\) is at least \(R_{\max}\), so the small-sample fallback in the definition of the cumulant-SVD estimator is inactive.

We first obtain the moment bounds needed for all subsequent uniform statements.  The treatment-loading, effect, and confounding bounds imply
\[
 |\alpha|\leq a_1,\qquad |\beta|\leq B,
 \qquad |\gamma|=|\alpha|\,|\gamma/\alpha|\leq a_1q_1. \tag{2}
\]
The structural equations can be written as
\[
 T_e=\alpha\epsilon_{u,e}+\epsilon_{t,e},
 \qquad
 Y_e=(\beta\alpha+\gamma)\epsilon_{u,e}
       +\beta\epsilon_{t,e}+\epsilon_y. \tag{3}
\]
For \(s=2R_{\max}+\delta\), the inequality
\[
 |x_1+\cdots+x_j|^s\leq j^{s-1}\sum_{a=1}^j|x_a|^s \tag{4}
\]
and the source moment envelope, applied to (2)--(3), give a finite constant \(K_W\), depending only on the fixed envelopes, such that
\[
 \sup_n\max_{e\in\mathcal E}
 \mathbb E\!\left[\|W_{e,1}\|^{2R_{\max}+\delta}\right]
 \leq K_W. \tag{5}
\]
In particular, every population moment and cumulant of \((T_e,Y_e)\) through order \(R_{\max}\) is uniformly bounded.  It follows that \(\|C\|\), \(\|c_k\|\), \(\|m_k\|\), and
\(\|h_k\|=\|m_k-\beta c_k\|\) are uniformly bounded for \(2\leq k\leq R_{\max}\).

We next construct the asserted first projections and control the degenerate remainders.  For random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_k\), the joint cumulant polynomial is
\[
 \kappa_k(X_1,\ldots,X_k)
 =\sum_{\mathcal P\in\Pi_k}
 (|\mathcal P|-1)!(-1)^{|\mathcal P|-1}
 \prod_{D\in\mathcal P}
 \mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j\in D}X_j\right], \tag{6}
\]
where \(\Pi_k\) is the finite set of partitions of \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\).  For a partition with \(s\) blocks, estimating its product of expectations by averaging the block monomials over \(s\) distinct observations and symmetrizing produces a symmetric \(U\)-statistic of order \(s\).  Hence each stipulated unbiased sample cumulant of order \(k\) is a fixed finite linear combination of symmetric \(U\)-statistics of orders at most \(k\), whose kernels have total polynomial degree at most \(k\).

Consider one such order-\(s\) statistic \(U_{n_e,s}(g)\).  Let \(g_j\) be its canonical centered projection of order \(j\), and define its first projection by
\[
 \psi_g(w)=s\{\mathbb E[g(w,W_2,\ldots,W_s)]-\mathbb E g\}.
\]
Successive subtraction of conditional expectations gives the exact Hoeffding identity
\[
 U_{n_e,s}(g)-\mathbb E g
 =\frac1{n_e}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\psi_g(W_{e,i})
  +\sum_{j=2}^s {s\choose j}U_{n_e,j}(g_j). \tag{7}
\]
Each \(g_j\) is degenerate in every argument.  Thus two summands in \(U_{n_e,j}(g_j)\), indexed by distinct unordered \(j\)-tuples, have covariance zero: conditioning on an index that occurs in only one tuple annihilates the product.  Therefore
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[U_{n_e,j}(g_j)^2\right]
 ={n_e\choose j}^{-1}\mathbb E[g_j^2]
 \leq K n_e^{-j}. \tag{8}
\]
The last inequality is uniform because the squared kernel has total degree at most \(2R_{\max}\), so its expectation is bounded by (5) and H\"older's inequality.  Since there are only finitely many orders, partitions, environments, and coordinates, (7)--(8) show that the sum of all terms of projection order at least two is \(O_{L^2}(n_e^{-1})\), uniformly.

Apply the deterministic signs defining each environment-versus-baseline contrast, and stack the resulting centered first projections.  This defines the arrays \(\psi^C_{e,n}\), \(\psi^c_{e,k,n}\), and \(\psi^m_{e,k,n}\); in particular,
\[
 \mathbb E[\psi^C_{e,n}(W_{e,1})]=0,
 \quad
 \mathbb E[\psi^c_{e,k,n}(W_{e,1})]=0,
 \quad
 \mathbb E[\psi^m_{e,k,n}(W_{e,1})]=0. \tag{9}
\]
Because \(n_e=n\pi_e\), equations (1), (7), and (8) yield, simultaneously over all relevant \(k\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sqrt n(\widehat C-C)
 &=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
     \pi_e^{-1}\psi^C_{e,n}(W_{e,i})+o_{L^2}(1),\\
 \sqrt n(\widehat c_k-c_k)
 &=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
     \pi_e^{-1}\psi^c_{e,k,n}(W_{e,i})+o_{L^2}(1),\\
 \sqrt n(\widehat m_k-m_k)
 &=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
     \pi_e^{-1}\psi^m_{e,k,n}(W_{e,i})+o_{L^2}(1).
 \end{aligned} \tag{10}
\]
Here and below, uniform \(o_{L^2}(1)\) means that the supremum of the second moment of the remainder over the stated arrays tends to zero.  Indeed, after multiplication by \(\sqrt n\), the bound \(O_{L^2}(n_e^{-1})\) in each environment is \(O(n^{-1/2})\) by (1).

Put
\[
 \nu=\min\{1,\delta/R_{\max}\}>0.
\]
Each first projection above is a finite sum of polynomials of degree at most \(R_{\max}\) in one observation, with uniformly bounded coefficients supplied by lower-order moments.  Conditional Jensen and (5) therefore imply
\[
 \sup_{n,e}\mathbb E\!\left[
 \|\psi^C_{e,n}\|^{2+\nu}
 +\sum_{k=2}^{R_{\max}}
 \{\|\psi^c_{e,k,n}\|^{2+\nu}
   +\|\psi^m_{e,k,n}\|^{2+\nu}\}
 \right]<\infty, \tag{11}
\]
because \((2+\nu)R_{\max}\leq2R_{\max}+\delta\).

We now linearize the generated projector.  Let \(P_C=CC^+\), where
\(C^+=(C^\top C)^{-1}C^\top\), so \(Q_A=I_{E-1}-P_C\).  The calibration gap gives
\[
 \|C^+\|=\sigma_d(C)^{-1}\leq\kappa_0^{-1}. \tag{12}
\]
For a perturbation \(H\) with \(\|H\|\leq\kappa_0/2\), every unit vector \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) satisfies
\[
 \|(C+H)v\|\geq\|Cv\|-\|Hv\|
 \geq\sigma_d(C)-\|H\|\geq\kappa_0/2,
\]
so \(\sigma_d(C+H)\geq\kappa_0/2\).  Expanding the inverse in
\[
 P_{C+H}=(C+H)\{(C+H)^\top(C+H)\}^{-1}(C+H)^\top
\]
by the exact identity
\[
 (G+D)^{-1}=G^{-1}-G^{-1}DG^{-1}
 +G^{-1}DG^{-1}D(G+D)^{-1}, \tag{13}
\]
with \(G=C^\top C\) and \(D=C^\top H+H^\top C+H^\top H\), and then collecting the terms linear in \(H\), gives
\[
 P_{C+H}-P_C
 =Q_AHC^+ +(Q_AHC^+)^\top+R_C(H),
 \qquad \|R_C(H)\|\leq K_P\|H\|^2. \tag{14}
\]
The constant \(K_P\) is uniform: (12) bounds the inverse of \(G\), the preceding direct singular-value bound controls the last inverse in (13), and (5)--(6) bound \(\|C\|\).

Taking \(H=\widehat C-C\), equation (10) and (11) give
\(\|H\|=O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})\) uniformly.  Hence the event on which (14) applies has probability tending to one uniformly, and its remainder is \(O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1})\).  On that event the rank-\(d\) SVD projector equals \(P_{\widehat C}\).  It follows that
\[
 \widehat Q-Q_A
 =-Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+
  -\{Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+\}^\top
  +o_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2}) \tag{15}
\]
uniformly.

By the already-established cumulant-cancellation lemma,
\[
 h_k=m_k-\beta c_k=\alpha^{k-1}\gamma u_k\in A=\operatorname{col}(C),
 \qquad Q_Ah_k=0. \tag{16}
\]
Consequently, the transpose term in (15) annihilates \(h_k\):
\[
 \{Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+\}^\top h_k
 =C^{+\top}(\widehat C-C)^\top Q_Ah_k=0. \tag{17}
\]
Write \(\widehat h_k=\widehat m_k-\beta\widehat c_k\).  Equations (10)--(17), together with the uniform bounds on \(\beta\), \(h_k\), and \(C^+\), show that
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sqrt n\,\widehat Q\widehat h_k
 &=\sqrt n\,Q_A(\widehat h_k-h_k)
   +\sqrt n(\widehat Q-Q_A)h_k
   +\sqrt n(\widehat Q-Q_A)(\widehat h_k-h_k)\\
 &=\sqrt n\,Q_A\{(\widehat m_k-m_k)
       -\beta(\widehat c_k-c_k)\}
   -\sqrt n\,Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+h_k+o_{\mathbb P}(1).
 \end{aligned} \tag{18}
\]
The last product in the first line is \(O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})\), uniformly, because each factor before multiplication by \(\sqrt n\) is \(O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})\).  Substitution of (10) into (18) gives
\[
 \sqrt n\,\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-\beta\widehat c_k)
 =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
   \pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,k,n}(W_{e,i})+o_{\mathbb P}(1), \tag{19}
\]
where
\[
 \zeta_{e,k,n}
 =Q_A\{\psi^m_{e,k,n}-\beta\psi^c_{e,k,n}
          -\psi^C_{e,n}C^+h_k\}. \tag{20}
\]
There are only finitely many \(k\), so the remainders in (19) are simultaneous.  Equation (20) also displays the same-sample estimated-plane correction, including its sign.

It remains to prove the uniform Gaussian approximation without imposing nonsingularity.  Stack (20) over \(d+2\leq k\leq R_{\max}\), and call the resulting fixed-dimensional vector \(\zeta_{e,n}\).  From (11), (12), and the uniform bound on \(h_k\),
\[
 \sup_{n,e}\mathbb E\|\zeta_{e,n}\|^{2+\nu}<\infty. \tag{21}
\]
Index the independent summands of the stacked \(Z_n\) by \(a=(e,i)\), and set
\[
 X_a=n^{-1/2}\pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i}),
 \qquad L_n=\sum_a\mathbb E\|X_a\|^{2+\nu}.
\]
Equations (1) and (21) yield
\[
 L_n\leq K n^{-1-\nu/2}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}n_e\pi_e^{-(2+\nu)}
 =K n^{-\nu/2}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\pi_e^{-(1+\nu)}
 \leq K' n^{-\nu/2}. \tag{22}
\]

For each \(a\), let \(G_a\) be an independent centered Gaussian vector with
\(\operatorname{Cov}(G_a)=\operatorname{Cov}(X_a)\), all the \(G_a\)'s being independent of all the \(X_a\)'s.  A Gaussian moment calculation gives
\[
 \mathbb E\|G_a\|^{2+\nu}
 \leq K\{\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}(X_a)\}^{1+\nu/2}
 =K\{\mathbb E\|X_a\|^2\}^{1+\nu/2}
 \leq K\mathbb E\|X_a\|^{2+\nu}, \tag{23}
\]
where the last step follows by applying Jensen's inequality to the convex map \(x\mapsto x^{1+\nu/2}\) and the nonnegative variable \(\|X_a\|^2\).  We now give a direct Lindeberg replacement bound.  If \(f\) satisfies \(\|f\|_\infty\leq1\) and \(\operatorname{Lip}(f)\leq1\), let
\(f_\varepsilon(x)=\mathbb E[f(x+\varepsilon Z_0)]\), with \(Z_0\) a standard Gaussian vector in the fixed ambient dimension.  Directly differentiating the Gaussian convolution gives
\[
 \sup_x\|D^2f_\varepsilon(x)\|\leq K\varepsilon^{-1},
 \qquad
 \sup_x\|D^3f_\varepsilon(x)\|\leq K\varepsilon^{-2}.
\]
Taking the minimum of the bound obtained from each display and using
\(\min\{A,Bt\}\leq A^{1-\nu}(Bt)^\nu\) shows
\[
 \|D^2f_\varepsilon(x)-D^2f_\varepsilon(y)\|
 \leq K\varepsilon^{-(1+\nu)}\|x-y\|^\nu. \tag{24}
\]
The integral form of the second-order Taylor remainder and (24) imply
\[
 |f_\varepsilon(x+v)-f_\varepsilon(x)-Df_\varepsilon(x)v
   -\tfrac12v^\top D^2f_\varepsilon(x)v|
 \leq K\varepsilon^{-(1+\nu)}\|v\|^{2+\nu}. \tag{25}
\]
Replace the \(X_a\)'s successively by the \(G_a\)'s.  Conditional on the sum of all terms other than the one currently replaced, the constant, linear, and quadratic terms in (25) have the same expectations because
\[
 \mathbb E X_a=\mathbb E G_a=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E[X_aX_a^\top]=\mathbb E[G_aG_a^\top].
\]
Thus telescoping, (23), and (25) give
\[
 \left|\mathbb Ef_\varepsilon\!\left(\sum_aX_a\right)
       -\mathbb Ef_\varepsilon\!\left(\sum_aG_a\right)\right|
 \leq K\varepsilon^{-(1+\nu)}L_n. \tag{26}
\]
Moreover, Lipschitz continuity gives
\[
 \sup_x|f_\varepsilon(x)-f(x)|
 \leq\varepsilon\mathbb E\|Z_0\|. \tag{27}
\]
Combining (26)--(27), then taking the supremum over the bounded-Lipschitz class, yields
\[
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\!\left(\mathcal L\!\left(\sum_aX_a\right),
                         \mathcal L\!\left(\sum_aG_a\right)\right)
 \leq K\{\varepsilon+\varepsilon^{-(1+\nu)}L_n\}. \tag{28}
\]
If \(L_n>0\), choose \(\varepsilon=L_n^{1/(2+\nu)}\); if \(L_n=0\), every summand is almost surely zero and the two laws coincide.  Equations (22) and (28) then prove uniform convergence to zero.

Finally, independence, centering, and \(n_e=n\pi_e\) show that the covariance of the Gaussian sum is exactly
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_aG_a\right)
 &=\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_aX_a\right)\\
 &=\frac1n\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}n_e\pi_e^{-2}
   \mathbb E[\zeta_{e,n}\zeta_{e,n}^\top]
 =\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\pi_e^{-1}
   \mathbb E[\zeta_{e,n}\zeta_{e,n}^\top]
 =\Sigma_n. \tag{29}
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(\sum_aG_a\sim N(0,\Sigma_n)\), and (28)--(29) establish the claimed uniform bounded-Lipschitz approximation.  No inverse eigenvalue of \(\Sigma_n\) entered the argument.  If \(\Sigma_n\) is singular, the Gaussian sum is supported on \(\operatorname{im}(\Sigma_n)\); if \(\Sigma_n=0\), it is the point mass at zero.  This completes every asserted part of the lemma.
